turn_text: This is Acropulse drive time for Thursday, June 20th, brought to you by the American Farm Bureau Federation. Good afternoon, I'm Jeff Nally. Iowa Senator Charles Grassley weighed in on the EPA's new tailpipe emission standards for light, medium and heavy duty vehicles in model years 2027 to 2032. The Iowa Republican believes the Supreme Court may soon weigh in on the EPA's regulatory authority.

But I think in the next two weeks, you're going to have the Supreme Court rule and change their Chevron doctrine from 1983 to a fact that the courts aren't going to accept a regulator's interpretation of the courts, and the courts have given a great deference to that under the Chevron doctrine, and if they overturn that, then that's going to put the courts back into being an honest interpreter of the law rather than just relying upon what the bureaucracy says.

Grassley voiced his concern as well over the volume of used cooking oil being imported into the US that's displacing US grown crops from the renewable fuel market and sending tax dollars to their overseas suppliers.

and I are asking the responsible agencies to verify that these imports and make sure that they're legitimate. We should not be subsidizing imports to harm our own local agriculture.

Use cooking oil or UCO imports have surged from 300 million to 3 billion pounds, displacing over 230 million bushels of soybeans that according to the National All Seed Processors Association. industry partners want verification that the imports are actually used cooking oil. Dan Bossy with Ag Resource Company says the industry needs a grade to qualify for used cooking oil.

I just want someone to scientifically tell me what used cooking oil is. Is there a measurement? Is there some scientific measure that we can go out and say okay this qualifies or this doesn't qualify? Today it's just a label and so until we come up with a scientific description of what used cooking oil is, and why millions of dollars of subsidy should be paid, I think the industry is leaving itself open.
Without a specific definition, Bassi says the market is open to abuse.

These cars are virgin palm oil with a French fry and a hot dog that are being passed along for subsidy. This is not right, but it's hurting American farmers because if we don't have an oil market that was supposed to be there because of renewable diesel, we're not going to get the bump in farm income that we had hoped.

AgriPulse publisher Sarah Wyatt spoke with Ted McKittie earlier today. Ted, the CEO of the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture. McKittie says they have a lot of different issues, but only one that stands above the rest.

Farm Bill is still the number one question. It's one that we take seriously, very involved, but tend not to be first in line on some of the more popular like the Title I commodities. So research and funding, getting back into some cadence of sustaining funding for research and facilities is one of ours. Trade is needing lots of attention. We're finding that through extensive international travel, us to those countries and those countries to the U.S. That's certainly in the mix. And then some other things. But Farm Bill and its many, many tentacles is probably at the fore.
Terrace are certainly a trade issue and McKinney says they do have a place.
There is a place for tariffs. There is. There has been for millennia. We can all debate on whether it's appropriate here.

However, there is one sure bet for countries that use tariffs. It's the certainty of trade retaliation that follows. This is AgriPulse drive time.
